entities.summary: Eugenius was a Roman usurper who briefly challenged the authority of the Tetrarchy in Syria in 303 CE. As a tribune commanding 500 soldiers from the Legio IV Scythica stationed in Seleucia Pieria, his spontaneous elevation by his troops represents one of the numerous, often short-lived, military insurrections that plagued the Roman Empire during periods of political instability. His rebellion, though quickly suppressed, underscores the fragility of imperial control and the persistent power of local military factions in the frontier provinces, particularly during the transition from Diocletian's first Tetrarchy to the later tumultuous period of imperial succession. His brief reign highlights the deep-seated tensions between central imperial authority and regional military power in the early 4th century.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Eugenius's brief usurpation is a minor, yet illustrative, event within the broader context of Roman imperial instability during the Tetrarchy, demonstrating the persistent challenge of military revolts to central authority. While quickly suppressed, it contributes to understanding the dynamics of power and succession in the early 4th century.
